facets.title: SRV Connection String (Atlas and DNS seedlist)

facts.text: SRV records provide automatic host discovery and TLS defaults. Atlas always provides SRV URIs. The driver resolves DNS SRV and TXT records to discover all mongos/replica set members.
Always set appName so ops teams can trace connections in server logs.
Use SRV connection strings for Atlas and any DNS-seedlist deployment.
Never hard-code credentials; use environment variables or a secrets manager.
Set compressors=zstd for bandwidth-sensitive workloads (requires server and driver support).
For serverless functions (Lambda, Cloud Functions), set maxPoolSize=1 and maxIdleTimeMS=10000 to avoid connection exhaustion.
Set retryWrites=true&retryReads=true explicitly in shared URIs for clarity (both are default since 4.2).

Each MongoClient maintains a pool of TCP connections per server (per replica set member or mongos). When your application requests an operation, the driver checks out a connection from the pool, executes the operation, and returns the connection.

facets.title: The Golden Rule: One Client Per Application

facts.text: Create a single MongoClient instance and share it across your application. The client is thread-safe (or goroutine-safe, or async-safe) in every official driver. Opening a new client per request is the most common pooling antipattern.
All drivers emit connection pool events for observability:
connectionPoolCreated / connectionPoolClosed
connectionCreated / connectionClosed
connectionCheckedOut / connectionCheckedIn
connectionCheckOutFailed / connectionCheckOutStarted
connectionPoolCleared
Subscribe to these events to track pool saturation, connection churn, and wait-queue depth.

Enabled by default since MongoDB 4.2. The driver automatically retries eligible write operations exactly once after a transient network error or a failover.
Eligible operations: insertOne, updateOne, replaceOne, deleteOne, findOneAndUpdate, findOneAndReplace, findOneAndDelete, insertMany (ordered or unordered), bulkWrite (ordered or unordered).
updateMany, deleteMany (not idempotent at the protocol level)
Writes with w: 0 (unacknowledged)
Individual writes within an explicit transaction (the transaction itself is retried)
RetryableWriteError - the driver retries automatically
NoWritesPerformed (MongoDB 6.1+) - both attempts failed without writing; safe to retry at app layer
TransientTransactionError - retry the entire transaction
UnknownTransactionCommitResult - retry commitTransaction()
Enabled by default since MongoDB 4.2. The driver retries eligible read operations exactly once after transient network errors.
Eligible operations: find, findOne, aggregate (without $out/$merge), distinct, count, estimatedDocumentCount, listDatabases, listCollections, listIndexes.
Let the driver handle retryable errors (retryWrites/retryReads).
Catch DuplicateKeyError (11000) for idempotent upserts.
Catch ServerSelectionTimeoutError for connectivity failures and alert.
Catch WriteConcernError when w: majority cannot be satisfied.
Catch MaxTimeMSExpired (50) and investigate slow queries.
Wrap bulk operations to inspect BulkWriteError.writeErrors array.
Log error codes, not just messages, for searchability.
Never swallow errors silently; always log or propagate.
Use transactions when business logic requires atomic updates across multiple documents or collections.
Prefer single-document atomicity when possible; redesign schemas before reaching for transactions.
Transactions are supported on replica sets (4.0+) and sharded clusters (4.2+).

Use withTransaction() (available in all drivers) instead of manual startTransaction()/commitTransaction(). The helper automatically retries on TransientTransactionError and retries commit on UnknownTransactionCommitResult.
If using manual control:
Transactions lasting >5 seconds (increases WiredTiger cache pressure and conflict risk).
Modifying >1,000 documents in a single transaction.
Using transactions for single-document operations (unnecessary overhead).
Not using withTransaction() helper (loses automatic retry logic).
Running DDL inside transactions (createCollection, createIndex).
Relying on transactions instead of redesigning schema for single-document atomicity.
MongoDB 8.0 introduced client-level bulkWrite() that can write to multiple collections and databases in a single network round-trip:
Use unordered for maximum throughput when order does not matter.
Batch sizes: the driver auto-batches into 100,000-operation groups. For very large imports, chunk at the application level.
Catch BulkWriteError and inspect writeErrors to identify which operations failed.
Use upsert: true in UpdateOne/ReplaceOne models for idempotent loads.
For multi-million-row imports, use mongoimport or mongorestore instead of driver bulk writes.
All drivers support collection.aggregate(pipeline, options). Key options:
Place $match and $project as early as possible to reduce documents flowing through the pipeline.
Use $match before $lookup to limit the join scope.
Set allowDiskUse: true only when necessary (large groupings/sorts).
Use maxTimeMS to prevent runaway pipelines.
Use $merge or $out for materialized views, not in-app aggregation.
Use explain('executionStats') to verify index utilization in $match stages.
Always persist resume tokens - store in a separate collection or external store for crash recovery.
Use fullDocument: 'updateLookup' when you need the complete document after an update.
Use fullDocumentBeforeChange: 'whenAvailable' (6.0+) for audit trails.
Filter early with $match in the pipeline to reduce network traffic.
Handle invalidate events (dropped collection, renamed collection) by reopening the stream.
For cross-collection CDC, watch at the database level: db.watch().
For cluster-wide events, watch at the client level: client.watch().
Files larger than 16 MB BSON document limit.
Storing files alongside metadata in MongoDB without a separate file service.
Accessing portions of large files without loading the entire file into memory.
Keeping files synchronized across distributed deployments.
GridFS stores each file as two sets of documents:
fs.files - metadata (filename, length, chunkSize, uploadDate, md5, contentType)
fs.chunks - binary data in 255 KB chunks (default), indexed by files_id + n
Use GridFS only for files >16 MB. For smaller files, store as BinData in documents.
Set appropriate chunkSizeBytes - smaller chunks for random-access reads, larger for sequential streaming.
Index fs.files on fields you query (e.g., metadata.author, filename).
Use streaming APIs (not readAll) to avoid loading entire files into memory.
Consider Atlas Data Lake or S3 for very large-scale file storage; GridFS is not a CDN replacement.
Use --file for repeatable scripts, not interactive copy-paste.
Use --quiet in CI/CD to suppress the mongosh banner.
Use printjson() for structured output; print() for plain text.
Store maintenance scripts in version control alongside application code.
Use --eval for one-liners in shell scripts and cron jobs.
mongosh supports full ES2022+: use async/await, destructuring, for...of, and template literals.
Use .mongoshrc.js for custom prompts, helpers, and default config.
Use this checklist when reviewing any application that connects to MongoDB:
[ ] Single client instance shared across the application
[ ] Connection string uses SRV format for Atlas / DNS seedlist deployments
[ ] appName set for observability
[ ] retryWrites and retryReads enabled (default since 4.2)
[ ] Write concern set to majority for durability
[ ] Read preference matches the use case (primary for consistency, secondary for read scale)
[ ] maxPoolSize right-sized for deployment environment
[ ] serverSelectionTimeoutMS set to a reasonable value (not infinite)
[ ] Graceful shutdown closes the client
[ ] Error handling catches specific error types, not generic exceptions
[ ] Duplicate key errors handled for idempotent operations
[ ] Transactions use withTransaction() helper with automatic retry
[ ] Projections used to limit returned fields
[ ] Indexes cover query patterns (ESR rule)
[ ] maxTimeMS set on long-running queries and aggregations
[ ] Change stream resume tokens persisted for crash recovery
[ ] Monitoring events wired to observability stack (pool events, command events, SDAM events)
